content.p: The Wah Ching began in 1964 as a handful of immigrant teenagers in San Francisco's Chinatown who wanted protection from the American-born Chinese classmates who bullied them. Over the following decades it became, in the words of police and prosecutors, a criminal organisation with branches far beyond the Bay Area. The name means "Chinese Youth".

The gang's reputation rests on a few well-documented events: a war in the 1970s that the San Francisco Chronicle says killed close to 50 people, the 1977 Golden Dragon restaurant shooting in which gunmen from a rival gang killed five bystanders, and a long series of investigations in Southern California. Much of what is said about the group comes from police reports and prosecutors, and some of it from memoirs by former gang members. Where a claim is an allegation, or comes from one source only, the account below says so.

Two accounts of the gang's start agree on its outline. Fair Observer, in an article adapted from the memoir "Chinese Playground" by former Joe Boys member Bill Lee, says a group of immigrant youths from Hong Kong and Macao came together in 1964 to defend themselves against American-born Chinese pupils at their middle and high schools. The group started with about a dozen members and grew fast. The Chronicle gives the same story: native-born Chinese youths tormented the newcomers, who were mocked as "FOBs", for "fresh off the boat", until the immigrants formed Wah Ching in 1964 and "the tables quickly turned".

Lee, quoted in the Chronicle, wrote that many of the founders "grew up on the rough streets of Hong Kong and Macao where gangs were hardcore" and that some had spent part of their youth in prison. Fair Observer's version of his account adds that retaliation against the American-born students was "fierce and brutal". These are the memoirist's descriptions, not court findings.

Lee told an interviewer for FoundSF that the Wah Ching was the first foreign-born gang in the neighbourhood, and that its creation changed the balance of Chinatown. Local gangs began to fight each other, and the tongs, the old benevolent and secret associations of the district, began to want muscle of their own. Fair Observer says some members broke away in 1969 at the urging of certain tongs whose elders wanted young recruits who spoke the language and honoured tradition. According to Fair Observer, the Wah Ching aligned itself with the Hop Sing Boys, a youth group that the tong's members called the Tornadoes in order to hide the connection.
content.h2: The Joe Boys and the Chinatown war
content.p: The enemy that defined the Wah Ching's 1970s came from inside it. Joe Fong, a former member, left the gang in 1971, according to the Chronicle. The paper says syndicate hitmen retaliated by shooting Raymond Leung, one of his best friends, at the corner of Jackson and Grant after a chase through the streets. Fong formed his own gang in 1972. Fair Observer dates the break to Chinese New Year 1972 and says Fong and his friends, who had belonged to another society called Yow Lay, adopted a new name that became "Joe Boys" on the street. The two accounts thus give Fong's path out of the Wah Ching differently.

On one side stood the Wah Ching and its syndicate allies, chiefly the Hop Sing Tong; on the other the Joe Boys. The Chronicle describes a run of killings in turn between them. The war was driven, it says, both by the wish to control Chinatown's profitable rackets and by plain revenge. Fair Observer counts an estimated 50 deaths from 1972 to 1978. The Chronicle says close to 50 people died in the 1970s, some chased through the streets and shot, some ambushed at home or work. Both numbers are estimates, and the sources do not list every victim.

Convictions were hard to obtain. The Chronicle writes that a code of silence governed terrified residents, and that even spouses of murder victims refused to talk. In Lee's account, quoted by FoundSF, people were afraid to go shopping or visit gambling halls, and there was a sense that the authorities saw only gangs killing gangs. By 1976, Fair Observer says, the Joe Boys numbered 150 to 175 and were fighting not only the Wah Ching but also the Suey Sing Boys and the John Louie Boys.
content.h2: Fireworks, graves and the Golden Dragon
content.p: The violence peaked around the trade in illegal fireworks. Fair Observer says American-born teenagers had sold fireworks in Chinatown before the Fourth of July since the 1950s, and that from 1972 the Wah Ching demanded protection money from the dealers and sold fireworks themselves, undercutting them. According to the Chronicle, the Wah Ching and Hop Sing had long controlled the trade in the Ping Yuen housing projects, and on the evening of 4 July 1977 the Joe Boys tried to muscle in. The paper says the attempt was bungled, partly because the attackers could not find parking, and that the Wah Ching were ready. Gunfire broke out in the streets. A 17-year-old Joe Boy named Felix Huey was shot dead in a stairwell, the Chronicle says. Fair Observer says two others were wounded; Lee told FoundSF that two Joe Boys and a Hop Sing member were hurt.

A second grievance followed. Fair Observer and Lee both say the Joe Boys found that the graves of dead members had been vandalised, which they took as a grave insult. Lee said in the FoundSF interview that the damage was blamed on the Wah Ching and Hop Sing. This is the Joe Boys' version, reported by a former member.

At 2:40 a.m. on Sunday 4 September 1977, at the height of the Labor Day weekend, three masked gunmen entered the Golden Dragon restaurant on Washington Street. The Chronicle reports that about 100 tourists and locals were inside. Among the diners were Michael Louie, a 20-year-old whom the paper calls head of the Wah Ching, and Frankie Yee, leader of the Hop Sing Boys. The restaurant was owned by the head of the Hop Sing Tong, Jack Lee, according to the Chronicle. The gunmen carried a semiautomatic rifle and shotguns, according to Fair Observer, and the shooting lasted about a minute.

They did not hit their targets. Five people died and eleven were wounded, and the Chronicle says none of the victims had anything to do with Chinese gangs. The dead were Paul Wada, 25, a law student at the University of San Francisco; Denise Louie, 20; waiter Fong Wong, 48; Calvin Fong, 18; and Donald Kwan, 20. Fair Observer says no gang member was wounded.

The shooting changed how the city treated Chinatown. Fair Observer says visitors stayed away, and business owners worried about tourism. Mayor George Moscone visited the district and raised the reward for information from $25,000 to $100,000, the maximum the city's law allowed. Police Chief Charles Gain announced a twenty-man Gang Task Force, first led by homicide chief Lieutenant Dan Murphy.

The Chronicle says the Chinatown unit was the first of its kind since the Chinatown Squad of the early twentieth century. Painstaking work and the reward, which it says went to an informant, led to the arrest and conviction of the three gunmen and their accomplices, except for the getaway driver, who was never caught. The Joe Boys disbanded. FoundSF describes the massacre as a turning point in Chinatown's gang history. The Chronicle says it marked the beginning of the end of the gangs' violent heyday. By the 1993 account of the Los Angeles Times, in the long contest for dominance in the 1970s "the Wah Ching won and the Joe Boys faded away".
content.h2: Killing of a leader and a Senate hearing
content.p: The Wah Ching's name returns in the early 1990s in connection with the killing of Danny Wong. The Los Angeles Times reported in November 1991 that Peter Chong, described as the reputed head of the Wo Hop To triad in San Francisco, repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment before a Senate subcommittee investigating Asian organised crime. Asked whether he was involved in the murder the previous April of Wong, the "reputed leader of the rival Wah Ching gang in San Francisco", Chong declined to answer. His lawyer criticised the subcommittee's conduct. The page does not say who killed Wong, and no charge against Chong for that killing appears in the sources opened.

In October 1993 federal officials unsealed a 48-count racketeering indictment in San Francisco against Chong, Raymond "Shrimp Boy" Chow and others, charging 19 reputed gang members in all. The Deseret News reported that it was the first time federal officials on the West Coast had used the federal RICO racketeering law against members of Chinese criminal societies. The pages opened do not link the Wah Ching to that indictment.

In Los Angeles the name appears in a different setting. A Los Angeles Times profile in August 1993 described Tony Young, 40, of Monterey Park, as the reputed head of the Los Angeles area Wah Ching, "a vast organized Asian gang with ties to international gangsters". Young, who said he was born in Shanghai and arrived in Los Angeles in 1969, called himself "just an average businessman" and said an extortion arrest in 1984 had brought charges that were never filed. The paper reported that he had never been convicted. According to the paper, a 1988 Justice Department report said he appeared to manage gambling operations for the Wah Ching, and a Senate subcommittee report listed him as having served under Vincent Jew, whom it identified as a former Wah Ching leader in northern California. His attorney, Harland Braun, called the police account a myth and a self-perpetuating rumour, and asked how Young could prove he was not the head of the gang.

A year later, authorities linked a gang rivalry in the San Gabriel Valley to the shooting deaths of two young people at a San Marino graduation party in June 1994. Sheriff's investigators told the Times that the rivalry pitted an older, highly organised ring of Chinese gang members against a new alliance of Filipino, Vietnamese and ethnic Chinese youths from Vietnam, with control of extortion rackets at stake. The Times said a woman whose son was allegedly a Wah Ching member was assaulted in Monterey Park two weeks before the report. Four people charged over the party shooting pleaded not guilty at arraignment. The article does not give the outcome, and it does not say the Wah Ching took part in the shooting.

In 2002 the FBI ran an undercover operation against the gang in the San Gabriel Valley. The San Gabriel Valley Tribune reported in October 2006 that four alleged leaders, known as dai-los or "big brothers", were expected to plead guilty to violent crimes in aid of racketeering. Kien Vay Luong, Paul Cho Liu, John Sun and Wai Yin Chu were arrested with seven other alleged members in 2002. The paper said the other seven had already pleaded guilty to charges ranging from firearms possession to murder, and that the four leaders faced a maximum of 20 years each. The FBI described the Wah Ching as a racketeering organisation responsible for murders, robberies, extortion and drug trafficking in the San Gabriel Valley and the Inland Empire, and said it was made up of four groups called "sides", each headed by dai-los. The long wait for trial was caused partly by an appeals court decision to suppress some wiretap evidence.

A local police lieutenant told the paper that the gang's presence had not changed, because a younger generation had stepped into the places of the men arrested. Police also said there had been no significant gang-related incidents since 2002 and that prostitution, drug dealing and white-collar crimes such as counterfeit software sales continued. Separately, the Whittier Daily News noted in 2010 that clashes between the Red Door gang and the Wah Ching in 2001 had been followed by several police arrests.

The name also turns up in individual crimes. In Orange County, a teenager who was a Wah Ching member, according to OC Weekly, fired five shots at Bowling Green Park in Westminster in June 2007. He was 17. The paper said he lost his jury trial in 2011 and was sentenced to the rest of his life in prison, with a further 25 years to follow. The paper said he wore a cap marked "MPWC", for Monterey Park Wah Ching, and had a tattoo of three round burn marks on a wrist.
content.h2: The gang in a later federal case
content.p: When federal prosecutors targeted Raymond Chow's Chinatown organisation in 2014, the Wah Ching came up again. Gangsters Inc., a crime-history site, said that in conversations recorded by an undercover FBI agent, a man named George Nieh described himself as leading the Wah Ching, a San Francisco street gang, while also belonging to the Chee Kung Tong and reporting to Chow. The site said prosecutors accused Chow, Nieh and four others of laundering $2,290,000 in purportedly illicit funds for the agent between March 2011 and December 2013. The Chronicle reported in November 2015 that Nieh had pleaded guilty, along with about a dozen others in the five-year investigation, including former state senator Leland Yee. Chow's lawyers said he had reformed and that agents had manufactured the crimes. The sources opened for this account do not cover the verdict in Chow's trial.
